cards.front: What is the grain of a fact table?
cards.back: What one row represents, stated in one sentence ("one row per order line"). Declare it before choosing columns.

cards.front: What does a fact table hold?
cards.back: Foreign keys to dimensions and numeric measures at the declared grain.

cards.front: What does a dimension table hold?
cards.back: Descriptive attributes of one entity (customer, product, date), wide and denormalized, with a surrogate key.
A star joins each denormalized dimension directly to the fact. A snowflake splits dimensions into sub-tables, adding joins for the same answer.
Warehouse-owned integer keys survive source key changes, allow several versions of a type 2 row, and an unknown member for missing references.
A dimension row (often key -1) that facts point to when the reference is missing, so inner joins keep every fact.
One that can be summed across every dimension: sales amount, quantity.
Summable across some dimensions but not time: an account balance or stock level. Over time take the last or the average.
A ratio or percentage: never sum it, recompute it from its additive parts.

cards.front: What goes wrong with mixed grain?
cards.back: An order-level value (shipping fee) repeated on each line is summed once per line. Allocate it or keep it at its own grain.
Overwrite the attribute in place: no history. For corrections or attributes nobody reports historically.
Close the current row (valid_to, is_current false) and insert a new version with a new surrogate key. Old facts keep the old version.
Keep the previous value in an extra column. Only one step of history.

cards.front: How do you select current rows of a type 2 dimension?
cards.back: is_current = true, or valid_to open (NULL or the end-of-time date such as 9999-12-31).
Same business key and event_date >= valid_from AND event_date < valid_to (half-open range).

cards.front: What happens if facts join a type 2 dimension on the business key only?
cards.back: Each fact matches every version of its customer and totals multiply.

cards.front: What is a late-arriving dimension member?
cards.back: A fact references a customer not yet loaded. Insert an inferred member (key plus placeholders) and complete it when the customer arrives.
One row per entity per period with its state at period end, such as stock per product per month.
One row per process instance (an order) updated as milestones happen (ordered, shipped, delivered dates).
Rows recording an event or coverage with no measure, such as products on promotion per day; counted or compared with sales.

cards.front: When do you need a bridge table?
cards.back: For many-to-many relationships (accounts with several owners), often with allocation weights so totals are not double counted.
The layer between tables and reports: relationships, measures, hierarchies and how filters flow.

cards.front: Default cross-filter direction from a dimension to a fact?
cards.back: Single: the dimension filters the fact. Both directions can create ambiguous paths and wrong totals.
One dimension used in several roles, such as dim_date for order date and ship date: one active relationship, the others inactive and activated in specific measures.
A compressed copy of the data in the model, refreshed on schedule. Fast queries, data as fresh as the last refresh.
Each visual sends queries to the source at report time. Fresh data, speed depends on the source.
A Fabric mode where the semantic model reads Delta tables in OneLake directly, without import refreshes.

cards.front: What is real in the BI Lab?
cards.back: Warehouse SQL runs on local DuckDB; star model checks are real queries; lineage is static analysis of SQL. There is no Power BI or DAX engine.
A predicate attached to a table so each principal reads only its rows, including inside aggregates.
Granting or denying SELECT on specific columns, such as DENY SELECT ON customers(email) TO support.
Query results show masked values to users without UNMASK. Stored data is unchanged; not encryption.

cards.front: Why is masking not enough on its own?
cards.back: Users can still filter on masked columns (WHERE salary > 100000) and infer values. Combine it with permissions.

cards.front: Unity Catalog row filters and column masks?
cards.back: SQL UDFs attached to a table (SET ROW FILTER) or column (SET MASK) that Unity Catalog applies on every query.
A dedicated service principal with only the grants the job needs, for example read on silver and write on gold.

cards.front: Why grant to groups rather than people?
cards.back: Joining or leaving a team changes one membership instead of many grants, and reviews are simpler.

cards.front: How does the Cloud Lab enforce T-SQL security?
cards.back: It rewrites each SELECT for its EXECUTE AS principal and runs it on DuckDB: T-SQL security translated to DuckDB, not SQL Server.
For each column, the source columns it is derived from, across views, models and reports.
Following lineage downstream to see which models and reports change if a column is renamed or redefined.
Any information relating to an identifiable person: name, email, customer id, IP address, and combinations that single someone out.
Yes. If re-identification is possible with additional information, GDPR still applies. Only anonymous data falls outside it.

cards.front: Why is an unsalted hash of an email weak protection?
cards.back: Anyone with a list of emails can hash them and join back. Use a secret key (keyed hash) or a lookup table kept apart.
Copy and expose only the columns a use case needs; it is a GDPR principle and the cheapest protection.
A join multiplies rows by the number of matches; duplicate keys on the "one" side inflate totals.

cards.front: Which error do you read first?
cards.back: The first failure and its innermost cause; later errors are usually consequences.
A filter on the partition column itself, so whole folders or partitions are skipped.

cards.front: Why select only needed columns on Parquet?
cards.back: Columnar files store columns separately; unselected columns are not read.

cards.front: Why are many small files slow?
cards.back: Fixed per-file costs (listing, opening, footers, tasks) dominate. Compact to roughly 128 MB to 1 GB files.

cards.front: Which columns make good partition keys?
cards.back: Low-cardinality columns that queries filter on, such as a date or region. Never a key with millions of values.
EXPLAIN shows the planned operators and estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and reports actual rows and time per operator.

cards.front: How do you compare two versions of a query fairly?
cards.back: Same data, several runs, one change at a time, and note whether caches were warm.
